title: Being Available Is How I Lost A Year (summermulder.substack.com), September 1, 2026
author: Summer Mulder
source: Summer Mulder's Substack (summermulder.substack.com), Summer Mulder's Substack
summary: Summer Mulder confesses that a free training community she promised roughly a hundred clients was never finished, because the blocked time she set aside to build it kept losing, day after day, to smaller incoming requests she answered immediately. She traces the habit to two motives she initially mistook for virtue: an unanswered question felt like an open loop she needed to close, and she wanted her team to see her working as hard as they were. The result was a founder who cleared everyone else's to-do list every day while her own most important, only-she-could-do-it work slid for over a year until the company closed. She argues this is not a headcount or staffing problem -- it shows up identically whether a leader has a full team or two contractors -- because the real issue is that every decision keeps landing back on the leader's desk, which looks like support but is actually a bottleneck. The piece closes on the single sentence that changed her behavior: something being urgent for someone else does not make it urgent for her.
points: Recounts a concrete failure -- a free client community left permanently unfinished -- as clean evidence of a chronic pattern of prioritizing others' immediate requests over her own most important work.
Identifies two disguised motives behind constant availability: treating unanswered questions as an intolerable open loop, and needing to visibly match her team's effort.
Argues the pattern is not about company size or headcount, since it reproduced identically with a lean team of contractors and a VA.
Reframes 'being responsive' as a bottleneck rather than support: when every decision waits on the leader, the team owns tasks but the leader owns every outcome.
Distills the fix into one operating principle: a request being urgent for someone else does not make it urgent for the leader.
quotes: I never finished the Skool community. We ran it free for our clients, extra support on top of what they were already paying for. I'd launched it with a few modules and about a hundred members had joined.

It sat on my list for over a year, sliding forward one square at a time, and I don't think there was ever a single day where I looked at it and decided not to do it. It just kept losing to whatever was in front of me.

I think about it more than the failures that cost money, because it's such clean evidence of a pattern that ran my entire working life. The thing only I could and should do got pushed. Every single time.

There was something else underneath it too, and it took me a long time to see. I wanted my team to know I cared as much as they did. If they had an idea for an email campaign, I wrote it that same day.

It shows up identically. You have two contractors and a VA. Every question comes to you. Every decision waits on you. It looks like support until you notice every decision is still sitting on your desk.
What finally changed it was one sentence I said out loud on a Thursday afternoon. It was urgent for them in that moment. That didn't make it urgent for me.
